speechtext:
Order, please. Proceedings under Standing Order 43. Before we proceed with the oral question period, may I say that hon. members probably are aware that I have received a notification from the Minister of Justice of his intention and desire to table a letter that I think has been referred to previously. In addition, in respect thereto I have received notices of intention by three ministers to raise a question of privilege. In all four instances there is an indication, with the letter that has come to the Chair, that because of the importance of the subject matter it would likely be in the best interests of relevant proceedings that these events take place prior to the question period. Of course, that would set aside the procedure which we have followed since last Easter.
May I first, therefore, indicate that I think it would be the desire of the House to accommodate that point of view in order to make for a more relevant question period. It would seem that the question period, if it were concerned with these events, would become somewhat of an anti-climax.
Therefore may I ask, before considering that request, whether or not the House gives its unanimous consent to allow the tabling of the document by the Minister of Justice and the proposed questions of privilege by these three ministers.
May I say to the House, before asking the House for its consent, however, that rather than attempt to follow each proposed question of privilege with a discussion by the House in respect of the question of privilege on its merits, it would seem to me that a more orderly procedure would be to Jake all three statements in respect of the notices of privilege given by the ministers, and then the Chair would have to decide, in order to accommodate the opposition in respect of the right it might ordinarily enjoy in those circumstances, either on a question of privilege or whatever content may develop, whether the Chair ought to extend its discretion at least in a question period which would run until, in my opinion, the matter had been thoroughly explored.
[DOT] (mo)
Possibly, depending upon the content of the declarations made by the minister in respect of the proposed questions of privilege, all the declarations might be followed by a statement by one spokesman for each party. But that is a
decision which will have to be made only after the House has heard the content of the statements. If the House is agreed on that general procedure, may I ask that hon. members give their unanimous consent to proceeding in that manner. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

sending immediately to Mr. Justice Aronovitch, which reads as follows:

Dear Mr. Justice Aronovitch:
Needless to say, I was very upset when I heard last week of the allegations to be published in the Globe and Mail that I had once interfered improperly in a case before you.
I am writing to express my appreciation to you for having acted quickly last week. As you know, once the facts were made known, the allegations about me were withdrawn by Mr. Justice Mackay.

Sincerely yours,
Jean Chretien.
I did explain myself in the House last Wednesday. If I annoyed Mr. Justice Aronovitch, I am sorry. As the member of parliament for the riding of Saint-Maurice who was confronted with a very difficult situation, and because I acted in good faith, I am sorry if I annoyed Mr. Aronovitch, but I did that for the purpose I explained to the House.

Mr. Speaker, I have read Mr. Justice Mackay's report to Chief Justice Deschenes on the circumstances of my visit to him, on March 8, 1970. I should like to make one or two observations.
First, I did not tell the judge that a telegram had been received by the Prime Minister from Prime Minister Williams, but that the Department of External Affairs had received a telegram from the Canadian High Commissioner, on Friday, March 6, transmitting a request from Prime Minister Williams that he be informed when the verdict could be expected. The Prime Minister of Trinidad stated that he made this request in view of his grave concern that riots and bloodshed would break out at that time.
Second, during my visit to Mr. Justice Mackay, I repeated to him the information available to us about the situation in Trinidad. I informed him of the request by Prime Minister Williams. In the course of our conversation, I also indicated to him that our High Commissioner had reported that the Governor General of Trinidad had called him to his office to inform him that he was most seriously worried about the situation. The Governor General of Trinidad expressed the hope that tempers would have time to cool down before the verdict.
Third my visit followed urgent representations made to the Prime Minister's Office by the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, late on Friday, March 6, informing us of those facts and requesting our assistance in order to determine the time at which the trial would be concluded. The Prime Minister was then on an official visit in the Arctic and was in the region of Igloolik and Spence Bay.
Fourth, my visit had no other purpose than to determine the approximate time when a verdict would be rendered

and I deeply regret that Mr. Justice Mackay may have interpreted my visit as aiming to delay the conclusion of the trial. I wish to state, without any reservation, that such was not my intention.
Fifth, I sincerely regret any embarrassment I may have caused Mr. Justice Mackay.
Sixth, I am grateful to Mr. Justice Mackay for stating his view that my visit "was clearly inspired by (a) great concern for the nation's interests and not by personal reasons".

-I did not think that he was attempting to influence my judgment.

Mr. Speaker, I think the event which concerns us this morning must be a landmark in the judicial history of our country. And I hope that after all the events of the last few days, today's discussions and actions will result in a warranty of the integrity of our judicial system all over Canada.
This morning, we heard excuses from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and also from the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) and we consider that these statements are made by responsible people, and I hope they did not go further than they said in their excuses.
This morning, we accept, not lightheartedly, the resignation of a minister. He is one of the ministers I admired most in the House for his honesty and integrity. This probably shows that we the people-I want to be the people's voice-see that the function of minister is not always a sinecure, that this function brings some responsibilities. Above all, the ministers being surrounded as they are by people who constantly clamour for more, I can understand that they, or hon. members, might be tempted to try and give more help to those around them who exert pressures ceaselessly. That is how I see the work the minister did with the judge, and I congratulate him for his action this morning; it is a guarantee for Canada that, among parliamentarians, there are still people who can
March 12, 1976

recognize that they may have gone too far, who can go back and bow before the requirements of public interest.
I do not wish to blame anyone this morning but I do blame our judicial system. That is where the evil lies. As long as it is not reformed, as long as appointments are political in nature, more specifically those of judges, they as well as ministers will at times be forced to act as some ministers are being accused of having done this morning.
I will say no more. But I do hope sincerely that the Judges Act will be amended in such a way that a judicial reform will be undertaken so that, at long last, we will have independent judges in a judicial system that is free of all political influence. In politics, there are games, and ministers do make promises as everyone does in times of elections-promises that are never lived up to-but the judiciary should never be mixed up with politics. In closing, I express the wish that a bill will be introduced to free judges from political influence.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a brief question for the Prime Minister. subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS OF MINISTER FOLLOWING RECEIPT OF CHIEF JUSTICE DESCHENES' REPORT
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think, as the Chief Justice points out, my duty is to see that the administration of public affairs is in accordance with the law. Accordingly, I have had the letter of the Chief Justice reviewed by the law officers of the Crown to determine whether it discloses any conduct constituting a wilful intent to obstruct, pervert or defeat the course of justice within the meaning of the Criminal Code or is conduct interfering with the course of justice amounting in law to contempt. I am advised there is nothing disclosed in the letter of the Chief Justice which dictates further action by me in accordance with my duties under the law and I have so advised the Prime Minister. It is of the utmost importance that this independence of the judiciary, achieved through great effort during the course of the last three centuries, be jealously guarded against all attacks.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ENSURE DEMOCRATIC RIGHT OF ELECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I introduce this bill because of the procrastination of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in calling by-elections. The purpose of these amendments is to ensure that the basic democratic right of representation of electors in a constituency in the House of Commons by duly elected representatives is maintained as fully as possible and that a minimum of time is allowed to elapse without proper democratic representation should a vacancy occur.
By these amendments, a maximum of 120 days shall pass between the time of receipt by the Chief Electoral Officer of the warrant for the issue of a new writ for the election of a member of the House of Commons to fill a vacancy therein and the polling date of the by-election to fill such a vacancy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Marshall (Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House the government must unilaterally proclaim its exclusive jurisdiction over a-200 mile coastal fisheries zone to stop critical depletion of Canada's fisheries resources.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to focus attention of the House on the serious problems confronting the fishery on both coasts of Canada. Although the motion speaks of a 200-mile coastal fisheries zone to stop critical depletion of Canada's fisheries resources, we support the extension of jurisdiction to the edge of the continental shelf and my party supports the government's stand on that matter. That position does not preclude our supporting a 200-mile coastal economic zone, or fisheries zone, in order to protect our depleting fisheries stocks. Other countries have realized the need to extend their fisheries limits. Most recently, the United States introduced legislation in the House of Representatives and the Senate to extend its fisheries limits. I feel that this is the right time for Canada to follow suit because our two great nations face common problems. Negotiations are going on between our two countries.
Incidentally, it is not my purpose today to criticize for the sake of criticizing. Hopefully, we shall make the government realize that time is of the essence, that the fishery is in a state of bankruptcy and that we cannot afford to wait longer. I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of State for Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) will put forward Canada's position at the Law of the Sea Conference to ensure that Canada will extend its fisheries zones in order to protect fish stocks which provide the livelihood of many thousands of Canadians.
The Minister of State for Fisheries is not present in the House. Yesterday he explained to me that he could not change his commitments. I accept that. I know his interest in the fisheries of Canada, and we do not hold him responsible for his absence from the House. I wish to first read from a booklet put out by the Department of External Affairs, entitled "The Future of the Oceans". It reads in part:
For the coastal fisherman, dependent on the stocks that in turn depend upon his home waters, overfishing by others can spell the end of his livelihood. This is where fisheries management comes in. The whole point of management is (ideally) to harvest the greatest yield that the complex of fish stocks in an area can replace annually. Only by applying management controls, such as quotas and seasonal limits (for example, during spawning), can the maximum yield be available each year to coastal fishermen and long-range ships alike.
I quote from the conclusions in the booklet:
The priority interests of the coastal state in all marine activities adjacent to its shores must be appropriately recognized and reflected in international law;
Fisheries
Much of the administration of the law of the future must be based on resource and environmental management concepts;
For any agreement to endure, there must be a better balance between the rights of individual states, whether flag or coastal, and the responsibilities which these rights carry with them regarding vital community interests in the uses of the sea.
The problem of extending our limits has been recurring each year. Everyone in Canada, with the exception of the federal government, agrees that we must take action to extend our limits in order to protect our fish stocks. The government is going a different route by having bilateral agreements with many nations. While we hope this will come about, they are taking the back route. The government should have extended the limits and then made bilateral agreements with other nations for economic and other purposes. To give some indication of the decrease in catches of fish stocks, I wish to quote from the Fisheries Prices Support Board 1974-75 annual report:
Preliminary figures indicate total Canadian landings of fish and shellfish, including freshwater fish, amounted to 1.9 billion pounds in 1974, a decrease of 14 per cent as against 1973. The landed value of $293 million represented a decrease of 9 per cent from the 1973 landed value of $320 million.
On the Atlantic coast landings were 1,532 million pounds in 1974, a decline of 14 per cent in weight and 1 per cent in value as compared with 1973. The decrease in landings was attributable to several factors including the over-exploited state of certain species, severe ice conditions late into the spring of 1974 and a six-week strike by the Newfoundland trawler fishermen during the summer of 1974. Groundfish accounted for 55 per cent of the total Atlantic Coast catch by weight and 45 per cent in terms of landed value.
Fish landings on the Pacific coast also dropped in 1974. The total landed catch on the west coast was 298 million pounds, a decline of 23 per cent by weight and 22 per cent by value as compared with 1973. Salmon landings amounted to 134 million pounds, a drop of 28 per cent in weight and 36 per cent in landed value as compared with 1973.
Government agency figures show that with regard to fisheries we are almost in a state of bankruptcy. Our fisheries' management is not at the level where we should brag about the fact that we are the best catchers and managers of fish in the world. It is surprising to note that in 1973 we imported $111 million worth of fish, and in 1974 $120 million. This is our own fish. It is fish we sell to other nations because we do not have proper management and processing facilities. We send it out of the country and buy it back at three or four times the price. That is not good, and must be corrected. However, we must first protect, conserve and control our resources which are vital to the livelihood of those in the eastern and western regions of Canada and, indeed, right across this country. I hope that when the minister replies-if there is time with all that is going on-he will give the House some indication of the direction that Canada intends to follow at the Law of the Sea Conference which begins next week.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext: When I called it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was attempting to discuss the effect of the continued restrictions and the need for placing quotas on many species of fish in Canada. It is a wonder to me that on the one hand-and I must give credit to the Minister of State for Fisheries because he is trying his best to give the infrastructure support to fishermen by way of small craft harbours and vessel subsidies-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext:
We are providing the subsidies and the infrastructure support, we are providing the vessels and the small craft harbours for the fishermen, but that at the same time, because of the depletion and deterioration of our stocks, we have on the other hand to give subsidies because there are no fish left. One course is certainly working against the other. For example, the minister announced the other day a $44 million temporary assistance program for Canada's troubled fishing industry. He is to be given credit for that. But I have to emphasize the point that on one hand we are giving bigger quotas through ICNAF to foreign nations which are taking away fish which rightfully belong to eastern Canada; then, when there are no fish, we have to pay the fishermen subsidies, and so on.
The other effect of the restrictions on fishermen is the destructive impact it is having on the morale of the fishermen, particularly in the Atlantic region. Every year another species of fish is added to those under quota. Every year-almost every few months-more regulations are established. Recently, one which caused great confusion right across the country was that which dealt with the lobster fishing rf;gulation. Then there is the restriction of the salmon catch and the provision for the licensing of boats. It is getting to the point at which the industry is fast becoming a police state fishery, and this is really having a harmful effect on the morale of the fishermen.
The incidents which arose just before the seal hunt are a perfect example of the fact that for the first time the peaceful fishermen of Newfoundland reacted, and about 200 appeared at a meeting designed to stop the "Greenpeace" organization interfering with their livelihood from the seal hunt. As the need for restrictions, licensing regulations and stricter regulations keeps coming forward, the fishermen are getting exasperated, disappointed, discouraged and will also react to the great deterioration and rape of our inshore and offshore fisheries and our banks fisheries. We go to ICNAF like a big brother and we allow them bigger quotas than we have ourselves. Our own fishermen are left without fish, without a livelihood, and they have to go on welfare.
The most recent problem which arises concerns the restrictions on the catching of red fish or ocean perch. I am sure my hon. friend from South Shore (Mr. Crouse) will elaborate on this aspect because it concerns him in Nova Scotia as much as it does me. But to show the reaction of Newfoundland, when it became necessary to restrict the catch of red fish to the Gulf of St. Lawrence, this is the

content of a telegram sent to the minister, of which I had a copy yesterday:
Restrictions on red fish fishing in the Gulf of St. Lawrence for the balance of 1976 will have a most damaging effect not only on the fish processors, plant workers and fishermen, but on the province's entire fishing industry.
It is obvious that officials of your department have been aware of the need for a reduction in gulf red fish landings from 1975 levels for some time and it is difficult to understand why this crucial factor was not taken into account in establishing 1976 ICNAF quotas last June at which time some 100,000 metric tons outside the Gulf were allocated to other nations with less than 20 per cent going to Canadian fishermen and requesting that any reduced red fish catch in excess of inshore requirements should be divided among all vessels fishing red fish on a pro rata base according to past fishing practices.
My hon. friend recommends that the federal government take steps to call a special session of ICNAF to raise the quotas established, especially outside the Gulf, to prevent the deterioration of the red fish section of the industry, and that Canada should withdraw from ICNAF because we are being locked into the present arrangement. I was sure, Mr. Speaker, that in the last few months the government was going to take the unilateral action which was so necessary.
It might be of interest to put on record some of the statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of State for Fisheries, as well as some of the experts in the Department of Fisheries and those who attend the Law of the Sea Conferences. I was very surprised at the ocean colloquium in Halifax to find our expert on the Law of the Sea, Mr. Beazley, so concerned and disappointed, and to hear him say that we would be continuing with Law of the Sea Conferences since we had come to no final conclusion. This was the first time I had seen him so disappointed and discouraged. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, speaking in Halifax, had this to say:
-an international solution is by far preferable to unilateral or even regional action. But time is of the essence ...
Should the Law of the Sea Conference fail or procrastinate, we will reassess all options ...
Unilateral action is one of the options open to the government of Canada-
That is what the minister said in February, 1975. Then the Minister of State for Fisheries, speaking in Geneva on April 29 of last year, had this to say:
Fishermen cannot eat negotiating texts.
Then on April 30, 1975, in announcing in Geneva that Canada would press for a 40 per cent cutback in foreign fishing efforts at the June meeting of ICNAF, he said:
I would find it difficult to ask fishermen to wait beyond the end of another conference ... It would be a question of determining what would be an unacceptable delay.
Then Mr. Lucas, one of our experts, speaking in Halifax had this to say:
The bottom line is that we cannot wait forever.
Then, again, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, on May 8 last in Geneva said:
Unilateral action is a more lively option today than it was after the Caracas session in 1974.
March 12, 1976

I would be less than candid ... if I were to leave you with the implication that we are entirely satisfied with the results of the conference.
Dr. Needier, head of Canada's delegation at the ICNAF meeting in Edinburgh on June 20, 1975 told reporters at the end of the session that in his opinion Canada might declare a 200-mile limit unilaterally within 12 months if no international agreement is reached. Then on July 22, 1975, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in this House:
I just want to remind the House that half of the European nations and others have exercised historic rights over what has been known for many hundreds of years as the high seas and a unilateral declaration of law as we see it would withdraw from these nations rights which they have been exercising, I repeat for hundreds of years.
They have rights, Mr. Speaker, but the Newfoundland fishermen also have traditional rights going back 600 or 700 years, and they are wondering what has happened to those rights. I am asking the minister to take this factor into consideration. Morale is worsening day by day and I cannot guarantee what is going to happen when the fishing season opens and foreign nations start fishing off our shores. I realize the minister has a problem, but we must extend our fishing limits at least for the time being, just as the United States has. Then we can have bilateral discussions on economic matters and on the continental slope.
When we do extend our limits-as I hope we will after the conference-we must also take measures to protect our fishermen. This is a matter I know the minister is concerned about, just as is the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) and the Minister of State for Fisheries.
The capability of Canada's air and sea rescue and lifeboat service and patrol aircraft is much less than desired. I should like to give the House an example of just what goes on in the Atlantic region. We have eight lifeboat bases in Newfoundland whose duty it is to protect and help save lost fishermen, as the name implies. On May 16, 1975, four new lifeboat bases were established, namely, in Shippegan, New Brunswick, Souris, Prince Edward Island, and Louis-bourg and Sambro, Nova Scotia. On the west coast of Newfoundland there is not one single lifeboat base. I should like to refer to a letter that I received from the executive assistant to the then minister of transport:
I am writing on behalf of Mr. Marchand in reply to your letter of May 21, 1975 in which you request that the Ministry reconsider its plan for basing 44 ft search and rescue lifeboats with a view to basing two of these lifeboats on the west coast of Newfoundland.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, two fishermen were lost out of Moreton's harbour. There is a lifeboat base at Twillin-gate, and I asked the minister what action that base had taken. I do not have the exact answer before me, but if I may paraphrase it, the answer was that unfortunately their 44-foot boat could not even go out because it is only capable of cutting through about two inches of ice. There are eight lifeboat bases, yet their boats can only cut through two inches of ice. I hope the minister will take these matters into consideration and discuss them with his responsible colleagues; and when he does extend the limit, as I know he will, I remind him that the fishermen must be protected and our air and sea rescue capability must be improved.
In view of the fact that time is short, Mr. Speaker, I will leave the rest of the wise advice that we are going to give the minister to my other colleagues.
Fisheries

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this discussion on the extension of Canada's fisheries jurisdiction. In a sense, I have no complaint with the motion itself; basically it suggests unilateral action as an option open to Canada in extending our fisheries' jurisdiction. In the motion itself there is no reference to the timing or the preparations that are necessary in order to undertake such unilateral extension. Indeed, there is no recognition or analysis in the motion or in the speech as to what the immediate effect would be for Canada and for Canada's fisheries if today the government accepted the invitation of the hon. member and extended, unilaterally, Canada's fisheries' jurisdiction. But I want to tell the hon. member, as I have said before, that unilateral action is one of the possibilities we have had under consideration and that it may be exercised at a time when it will achieve real advantages for Canada.
21419 -52V1

March 12, 1976
Fisheries
The hon. member, in his speech, said we ought to do it right away. I think that was more of an encouragement of the government to continue its efforts than a clear decision on his part that action ought to be taken at this time. The Law of the Sea Conference is opening on Monday. It is a crucial conference for Canada. The hon. member probably will be present, as I will be present, at the conference next week. We will make every effort to make progress on all the issues affecting Canada, but particularly on the fisheries issue because we know, as the hon. member has pointed out, that the fisheries need protection on the east coast and on the west coast. On the east coast, stocks of fish that are vital to the future of Canadian fisheries are seriously depleted. That is the underlying concern behind the energetic efforts that are being undertaken by my colleague, the Minister of State for Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc), by his officials and by my officials in a variety of ways.
On the west coast, the new emerging regime of extended jurisdiction is also necessary and any future regime must take into account the special problem of the salmon fishery which is of importance to the west coast of Canada. We have not been idle. As the hon. member knows, there has been action over the years-action which the government of Canada has taken sometimes unilaterally and sometimes ahead of other countries. First, in 1964 the government unilaterally extended Canada's fishing limits to 12 miles. That is taken for granted today, but at that time it was a very important step ahead. We found that countries which has opposed us in taking that unilateral step quickly followed in adopting the 12-mile limit. Second, in 1974 we went a step forward and closed the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the Bay of Fundy, Queen Charlotte Sound, Dixon Entrance and Hecate Strait as exclusive Canadian fishing zones. These waters are so extensive that they would exceed the 200-mile area of many countries.
In taking that action, we negotiated a phasing-out of the operations of fishing fleets of other countries and today they are almost at the end of their participation in these waters. Last year, as a third point of our emphasis on the importance of the fisheries, we took very strong action in closing the Atlantic ports to the Soviet fishery fleet, with beneficial results in terms of the acknowledgement by the Soviet Union and other countries of the serious overruns that had been taking place in the catch of fish.
Of course, at ICNAF as well we were able to secure a 40 per cent reduction in foreign fishing efforts in respect of ground fish, as well as a reduction in the total allowable catch of depleted stocks and higher quotas for Canadian fishermen in respect of particular stocks which are important to them. These have been important actions. We do not, however, regard them as a substitute for extended Canadian fisheries which we still have as a primary objective of Canadian policy. In my opinion, Canada will soon have a fisheries zone of 200 miles.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext:
The hon. member overlooked mentioning my most recent quote on this subject which was made last weekend: I said it was not a question of "if", but a question of "when". We want to take action at a time when it will be effective and at a time when it will be timely.

There is no doubt that we have made progress at the Law of the Sea Conference. Unfortunately, we have not made progress rapidly enough to wrap up an over-all treaty including a definition of the jurisdiction of coastal states over their extended jurisdictions. But the single negotiating text that came forward at the conclusion of the last Law of the Sea Conference included most of the concerns Canada has had in respect of the fisheries, and met most of our fisheries' objectives.
At this particular conference we propose to build upon that text and to make further progress where possible in order to solidify, in the text and in the understandings, the position of the Canadian government. I have always said it is the preference of the government of Canada to have its extended jurisdiction, the 200-mile economic zone, accepted as part of an over-all, multilateral settlement engaging in and involving all the countries of the world. In addition to the question of the 200-mile economic zone, there are other various interests involved, including the proper role of salmon and also a host of interests affecting Canada. At the present time, at the Law of the Sea Conference all these issues are treated as a package. Up to the present time, few countries have been ready to settle on the fisheries alone until they know how their interests will be treated in all the other aspects of the conference.
So far as Canada is concerned, we would be prepared, if it were possible, to settle on a treaty at an early date that would include provisions that we find acceptable with regard to the fisheries, provided it would not at the same time prejudice other important Canadian interests. We would be prepared to do that. I am doubtful, however, whether it will happen at this particular Law of the Sea Conference.
In addition to the conference which is beginning in New York next week, it is our expectation-and indeed our firm desire-that the conference in New York be succeeded by a further conference in the summer to carry forward the work that has been accomplished in New York. At the end of that conference, although we know progress will be made, we are not quite certain, at this point, of the extent of the progress but we will be working with other delegations to bring off the greatest possible success. Hon. members who have attended these conferences know that the Canadian delegation has continually played an innovative and responsible role at the conference, and it will be working actively at the upcoming conference to ensure that the provisions that emerge are equitable, effective and responsive to current needs and realities. That is one aspect of the situation and it is an important one. We will be watching results there to determine what course of action we might take.
At the same time, we have been negotiating bilateral agreements with distant fishing countries exploiting the waters which at some future time will be under Canadian jurisdiction. Just yesterday we initialled a further agreement with Portugal, an agreement which of course is initialled ad referendum but which deals with Portuguese fishing in our 200-mile zone.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext:
What did you give up for it?
March 12, 1976

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext:
That is the fourth bilateral agreement that we have succeeded in negotiating, at least ad referendum in the case of Portugal. Previously we had achieved similar results with Norway, Poland and Spain, and negotiations are under way with the Soviet Union. I hope they can be completed successfully in the near future. We have had discussions with the Soviet Union, and we hope that we will have a further round of meetings with them in May. If we succeed in getting a bilateral agreement with the Soviet Union, it will be quite dramatic progress because, having concluded and initialled an agreement with other countries and now with the Soviet Union, we will have covered a substantial portion of the fishing catch of foreign countries in an extended 200-mile zone. I will come back to that in a moment.
What do these bilateral agreements contain? They are all based on the elements of the emerging consensus of the Law of the Sea Conference. Under these agreements, when Canada extends its 200-miles it will be Canada that decides the total allowable catch from each stock; it will be Canada that determines the stocks that may be surplus to Canadian requirements; and it will be Canada that decides the allotments for the foreign fleets from these surpluses. These are the provisions in these agreements.
The four countries that I have mentioned-namely, Norway, Poland, Spain and Portugal-include 30 per cent of the fishing catch of foreign fleets in this extended zone. When we conclude the agreement, as I hope we will, with the Soviet Union, 88 per cent of the fishing catch in these waters by foreign fleets will have been covered by bilateral agreement. That is a major achievement and it is very much related to the question of unilateral jurisdiction, or the extension of unilateral jurisdiction, because if and when we extend our jurisdiction we will have in place, with the major countries now fishing in these waters, agreements that will recognize Canadian extended jurisdiction and the ability of Canada to decide the total allowable catch, to decide what Canada would take, what is surplus to Canada's requirements and how that surplus will be allotted among foreign fishing fleets. It seems to me that it is a very good thing to have these agreements in place before Canada takes a unilateral action and is faced with the problem, for example, that Iceland is presently facing in implementing its unilateral extension of the 200-mile limit.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext: Iceland has no problem. She demonstrated she can take on Her Majesty's fleet.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext:
I do not want to get into a discussion on Iceland's position and the British position, but it is a fact that the Icelandic government has taken action to extend its jurisdiction to 200-miles. They say, now, that we should control these waters in so far as fisheries are concerned, and the British government has stated that these are international waters and they do not recognize Icelandic jurisdiction and intend to continue fishing there. Now both countries are involved in an effort to negotiate an agreement which will accommodate the interests of both countries in an extended Icelandic jurisdiction.
What we have been doing is to arrive at these agreements before the extension is undertaken, rather than afterwards, in an effort to avoid the futile, sterile and
Fisheries
dangerous confrontation that might take place if we proceeded unilaterally without having in place this kind of agreement. I believe that if in May we succeed as I hope we will in negotiating this agreement with the Soviet Union, we will have put in place a groundwork and a foundation that will make an extension of our jurisdiction effective when it does take place. I believe hon. members will recognize that as being an extremely important aspect of Canadian fisheries' policy.
The hon. member has properly referred to the effect on Canada if other countries extend their jurisdiction prior to Canada doing so. Obviously, we are watching the probable timing of extension by other countries. It is expected that the Mexican 200-mile economic zone, including not only fisheries but minerals, marine pollution and marine scientific research, will come into effect in June. A number of developing countries have enabling legislation so that they will be able to extend their 200-mile fishing zones at a relatively early date. Of course, we are all watching what is happening in the United States where it is expected there will emerge soon, from the congressional conference committee, which is now reconciling the House and Senate versions of the bill, a final version which will probably establish an effective date of enforcement of United States jurisdiction early in 1977.
We do not know what the date will be. One bill called for January 1, 1977, another the middle of the year, and the effort is to reconcile them. We do not know what will happen, but probably it will be an effective date of early 1977. We are taking steps to ensure that any U.S. extension will not affect the continuing right of Canadian and U.S. fishermen to enjoy reciprocal fishing privileges in each other's zones, and that our position on unsettled Canada-United States maritime boundary questions will not be prejudiced by any such action. These include such unsettled questions as the Gulf of Maine area, off Juan de Fuca Strait and off Dixon Entrance. So it is obviously realized by hon. members that negotiations with the United States on fisheries are a crucial part of our preparations for the extension of fisheries jurisdiction, and as a neighbouring coastal state there are special concerns to be taken into account. Canadian fishermen fish off the United States coast, and vice versa, and their interests are important. Some fish stocks migrate up and down the coast, and these must be properly managed. We must also try to ensure that there will be no problems of enforcement in the new zone, both as between our two countries and vis-a-vis third countries.
There is also the special problem of salmon fishing by both countries. All these problems are complex and difficult which exist and which must be resolved between Canada and the United States. Consultations have begun and I am sure solutions will be found. A great deal of attention has been focused on the legislation in the United States. It should not be forgotten that in Canada no new enabling legislation is required. We are ready to move on very short notice, because under the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act our extension of fisheries jurisdiction can be accomplished after giving 60 days' notice by order in council. So we do have legislative authority from parliament. It requires executive action and after 60 days' notice

March 12, 1976
Fisheries
an effective date of enforcement can come into play. So we are prepared legislatively. We have been preparing, through our discussions with the distant fishing states, for the eventual extension of our jurisdiction.
I have already stated that extended Canadian jurisdiction is a certainty. It is not in the distant future. I regret that I cannot give a precise date, but it is a certainty and it is not in the distant future. It will depend upon a number of factors, including the progress made at the Law of the Sea Conference, the further success made in our bilateral negotiations with other countries, and also the steps taken by other countries, especially our friend and neighbour the United States.
I want to assure the hon. member that the government is quite alive to the urgency of the seriously depleted stock situation on the east coast. It is quite alive to the concerns of west coast fishermen. A firm and stated objective of our policy is to achieve extended fisheries jurisdiction at the earliest possible date, and we have placed ourselves in a position to bring it off in a timely and effective way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate today seems to be more a case of agreement than of confrontation. As the Secretary of State for External (Mr. MacEachen) has pointed out, the question is not "if," but "when" Canada is to extend its control over the fishing areas off our coasts. I regret that the experts in this field in our party, the hon. member for New Westminister (Mr. Leggatt), the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) and the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) are all away this afternoon, leaving it to me to speak briefly on our behalf. I may say that I had also hoped that the leader of our party, who was in Newfoundland a few days ago dealing with these very matters, might be able to take part, but he, too, is tied up.
I want to indicate our support of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), and I am glad to note that the Secretary of State for External Affairs regards it as a motion of encouragement rather than argument.
I must point out to the hon. member that last June, I believe it was, we had a debate on a similar subject when a motion was put down by the then member for St. John's West. He called for the extension of our control out to the end of the continental shelf and we had to point out that he forgot to mention the 200-mile zone. Today, my good friend, the hon. member for Humber-St. St. Barbe has put on a motion calling for control out to the 200-mile limit and he forgot to mention in his motion the continental shelf. However, in his speech he made it clear that he means both, and we are supporting his intention, not just the words of the motion.
I also welcome the statement which has been made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in which he quite properly referred to the bilateral agreements which have been achieved and to the fact that if Canada is able to achieve one with the Soviet Union, we will be awfully close to having a 200-mile zone so far as Canada is concerned. One has to say that the minister is doing a good job in that regard, and I want also to join the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe in paying tribute to the

good job being done in this field by the Minister of State for Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext:
In fact, I hope it will not hurt him if I suggest he is doing such a good job that he should not be a minister on half pay. He should be a full minister because of the efforts he is making on behalf of the fisheries industry of this country.
I think we are all aware of the fact that the reason something has to be done about the fishing areas off our coasts, both east and west, is because at the present time, when we only have a 12-mile limit, fleets of foreign vessels are engaged in massive fishing operations to such a degree that they are fish mining rather than just fish harvesting. They are treating fish not as a renewable resource but as an ore to be removed and processed, and let that be the end of it. The result of this, of course, is that there has been a tremendous decline in fish harvesting by our Canadian fishermen, a tremendous decline in the landings and, what is even more serious, a decline in the stocks. The situation has reached the point where something has to be done about it very soon. I think the most serious problem is on the east coast, as has been indicated by both previous speakers, but there is also a special problem on the west coast, particularly in respect of the salmon fishery.
We are aware of the fact that the Law of the Sea Conference will resume this coming week in New York city. I had hoped that the minister might be able to express his confidence that out of that conference would come an agreement on a 200-mile zone or a continental shelf. At least he is keeping his options open in that respect. It is still our view, along with the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, that if agreement on that is not reached, Canada should still assert its intention, even if we have to do it unilaterally, of going for a 200-mile zone or a zone out to the end of the continental shelf.
When the day comes that we do get control over the waters on our coast, we want to emphasize, of course, that in addition to the control of fishing in those waters which would give Canada the right to say how much we would take and how much would be available for other nations, the day must also come when we should have control over pollution in those waters, control over the right of passage, control over scientific research. In other words, there are a number of other matters in relation to the actual fisheries that are of concern to us in the areas off our coasts whether 200 miles or out to the end of the continental shelf.
So, Mr. Speaker, we express our pleasure that this motion has been put down today. We express our pleasure that there is agreement amongst us that the principle proposed in the motion is one that has to be implemented in one way or another. We hope the seriousness of the matter, in terms of not letting time go by, will impress itself upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of State for Fisheries and that action in this area will be taken with the least possible delay.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate on
March 12, 1976

Canadian fisheries. Much of the constituency that I represent in this House depends in whole or in part on the economic future of this important primary industry. Throughout Atlantic Canada it is estimated that some 20,000 fishermen and 12,000 plant workers depend on the fishing industry for their livelihood. Naturally, when this industry suffers economic hardship or sets sail on the wrong course, members of parliament representing Atlantic Canada are soon made aware of the fact. It is our responsibility to try to assist those who look to us for guidance and leadership.
With each passing day I begin to have a clearer realization of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) meant when he said that when members of parliament get 50 feet from Parliament Hill, they are nobodies. It would appear that not only the Prime Minister subscribes to that belief, but it is also held by ministers of the cabinet and other ministers of the Crown as well as the Minister of State for Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc). Let us consider, for example, the announcements that have been made outside this House by the Minister of Fisheries when he is, in effect, by ministerial decree, altering the lives and livelihood of thousands of Canadians in Atlantic Canada.
On December 30, for example, the minister issued a news release announcing tighter controls on the east coast lobster fishery. This announcement could well have been made prior to the adjournment of the House for the Christmas recess, when the representatives of the people would have had an opportunity to respond to these arbitrary new measures which have caused heartache and hardship to hundreds of lobster fishermen in Atlantic Canada this year. Heaven knows how many will be affected next year.
The minister's opening line of, "New measures coming into effect today to exclude from the lobster fishery those who earn their living elsewhere", was enough to cause consternation among all lobster fishermen, for each and every one of them earn part of their living doing some other work besides lobster fishing. I submit it is desirable to get the doctors, the dentists, the lawyers and the professional people out of the lobster fishery, and almost everyone agrees with this. The minister obviously failed to realize, however, that in our mixed economy it is necessary for many men and women to work at different trades in order to provide for the financial needs of their families. For example, here is a typical letter from a constituent residing in Lockport, Shelbourne county, which I should like to put on the record. It is dated January 1, 1976, and he writes:
I received a letter saying my lobster fishing licence would not be renewed in 1976, as I don't make my living at fishing, that I have a full-time job. I don't think working at a fish plant can be called a full-time job. I have to work all hours of the day or night in order to make between $5,000 and $6,000 (before deductions) at a fish plant. Therefore, I depend on lobster fishing for part of my income. I don't think any fisherman makes this small income for a year. It seems very odd to me that a Canadian can't make a living for himself yet foreign vessels are allowed to come into Canadian waters and take whatever kind of fish they want and destroy the fishing grounds.
He finishes by saying:
I would like to know why my lobster licence will not be renewed in 1976. What crime have I done? If it's a crime to try and make a living, then I am guilty.
Fisheries
I am withholding the writer's name, but this is indicative of many letters I have received concerning this matter. Even bona fide fishermen were concerned with the wording of the minister's letter. In addition to lobstering, many of the fishermen, if not all of them, haul and paint their own boats, thereby infringing on the shipyards which depend upon refitting ships for part of their livelihood. Others paint their own homes or maintain market gardens, thereby earning part of their living from moonlighting as farmers or housepainters. Under this government it is apparently acceptable for Canadians to moonlight in some fields, but is not acceptable to moonlight in others. This double standard has not been lost among all lobster fishermen, those who have their licences this year and those whose licence has been denied.
As far as I can determine, most lobstermen were opposed to the procedure being followed: they were not opposed to the end to be obtained. It would have been more humane and just, in my view, to let attrition within the industry take its course. If licensed fishermen stopped fishing for more than one year, other than those who could not fish due to illness, then the licence should not be renewed.
I submit there are other steps that should be taken, Mr. Speaker. Steps should be taken to restock lobster fishing areas. This could be done by the fisheries department offering to pay a premium for seed or berried lobsters landed by our offshore or inshore lobster fishing fleets. These seeded lobsters could be returned to the sea by our fisheries officers, thereby helping to build up depleted stocks. Money spent in this manner would be a positive step toward rebuilding this very important segment of the industry.
Parliament was in session on February 11 when the Minister of State for Fisheries announced outside this House a modified fisheries assistance program. The House was also sitting on March 3 when he announced the closure of the Gulf of St. Lawrence red fish fishery. The continued refusal by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), ministers of the Crown and the Minister of State for Fisheries to appear before the peoples' representatives to explain what they are doing and to make statements which gravely affect the livelihood of Canadians is, at best, arrogant and, at worst, unmitigated gall. When this course is followed we, in the official opposition, who are elected to parliament, have no opportunity to comment, to amend, to suggest or to improve the minister's dictatorial statement.
I accept that the minister cannot be here today. The minister may say we are debating the statement today; but now it is fait accompli. The gulf closure is in effect, as of March 6. Those affected by this decree must suffer the economic hardship emanating from this action. One thing is certain. The Minister of State for Fisheries will go down in the history of Atlantic Canada as one who closed more fisheries industries than any previous minister in our history.

speechtext:
As one of my seafaring constituents said to me, "When policies are required to help Canadian fishermen, the minister sure has a hole in his seabag." Many of my constituents also ask when we are to see the appointment of a full-time minister of fisheries, as promised by the Prime Minister and other cabinet ministers in Nova Scotia and Atlantic Canada during the 1974 election campaign. I can only answer that obviously the Prime Minister does not give high priority to the fishing industry or to his promises once the election campaign is over.
Anyone who compares Liberal promises made to Atlantic fishermen during the 1974 campaign with the record of the government to date will gain some idea of the deceit and deception practised on our people by the government. I say this to the government: you promised, for example, to expand the area within Canada's jurisdiction for fisheries to the edge of the continental edge and slope, or 200 miles, whichever is greater; you said this will be achieved through action at the international conference on the Law of the Sea at Caracas. The Caracas conference concluded without action being taken. We witnessed the Geneva conference of last March. There was no international agreement. We now know that another conference will open on Monday in New York.
According to a report in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of Wednesday, March 10, the Canadian government does not expect the next Law of the Sea conference, which opens in New York on March 15, to succeed in producing any international agreement. Realistically we do not expect that any over-all law of the sea treaty will be completed at New York. That was the opinion of External Affairs officials. The minister endorsed that statement today in his speech made to the House. So we have promises but no action. While we are jawing other nations are warring on our fisheries resources and depleting them below sustainable yield levels. That is the reason for our motion today. We are simply asking you, the government, to take the action you promised more than two years ago.
The Minister of State for Fisheries said at last year's conference in Geneva that time is running out on this issue, that fishermen cannot eat negotiating texts, and that fish stocks cannot be rebuilt on negotiating texts. He made the headlines, and I supported him in his views. But I point out to the minister that we require action, not words, to bring about a solution to our problems. We need only look at the decline in total fish landings in the Maritimes for 1975 to realize the severe effects of massive over-fishing by foreign fleets on our fish stocks during the last ten years.
Total fish landings were down to 889 million pounds from 905 million pounds in 1974. Obviously, unless the Minister of State for Fisheries and the government move quickly to declare a 200 mile fishing zone on our continen-
tal shelf, the fishing industry of Atlantic Canada is doomed to economic collapse. The wreckage of its destruction must be placed squarely on the backs of the present federal government. The government alone has the responsibility, the obligation, and the power to act. By refusing to act the government stands indicted not only by the people of Atlantic Canada but indeed by all Canadians. It is responsible for allowing the collapse of this industry which is the mainstay, literally, of thousands of Canadians in an area with few alternative forms of employment.
You promised to provide means for proper offshore surveillance. You would do this by increasing the number and size of our fisheries patrol vessels. This has not been done. Only yesterday we learned in the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, from the Minister of State for Fisheries, that in order to carry out fisheries surveillance the department was forced to employ oceanographic and fisheries research vessels at a cost of $360,000. While this was going on the normal work of these ships was not being done, which accounts for the spotty oceanographic work and the lack of research carried out by the department prior to making decisions which have a detrimental effect on the economy of Atlantic Canada.
You promised in the 1974 campaign that our fisheries resources, to the maximum extent possible, would be harvested, processed, and marketed by Canadians. The truth is that foreigners are still harvesting the largest percentage of the stocks taken from our waters.
You promised to provide additional financial support for the construction, conversion, and modification of fishing vessels. Yet in actual cases some fishermen have built new boats and are still waiting for subsidy payments.
You promised to provide improved marine facilities, such as wharves, breakwaters and haul-outs, under your small craft harbour policy, and pledged a budget of $30 million for the fiscal year 1974-75. It was to be maintained for four years. What happened? The very first year, when cuts had to be made, you did not cut down on the CBC, or on the National Art Centre, or on CIDA aid to Cuba; but you did cut from $30 million to $20 million your program of assistance-

Or, let the minister be quiet and make his contribution at the proper time.
The government promised to develop our recreational fisheries through the rebuilding of fisheries stocks. It was to build hatcheries and spawning channels. So far all that the government has done is close down the fish hatchery at Kedgemakooge. I could go on and on. The list of broken promises is endless.
Frankly, the statement of the Minister of State for Fisheries establishing a quota of 30,000 tons of redfish for the 1976 Gulf of St. Lawrence fishery is totally unacceptable to the members of the official opposition. I say it is unacceptable because it is unjust, divisive, and indefensible. It is an unjust policy. The basis on which these quotas is established is false and deceitful.
To date the large trawlers owned and operated by Nova Scotians and Newfoundlanders landed approximately one half of all the redfish processed by plants in Prince Edward Island, Georgetown and Shippegan. The tonnage landed at these points came from only part of the fleet operating and based in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. By using the landings of the entire Canadian Atlantic fleet as a basis the government is setting up arbitrary quotas for the catching of redfish which apply only to those ships based in St. Lawrence River ports.
I say this closure is unjust because Nova Scotia, for example, has already landed most of its allowable quotas during the months of January and February. This, really, is a retroactive ruling. It does not permit the Canadian companies affected any time to plan or reorganize their operations. It is unjust because it works its greatest hardship among Canadians, ashore and afloat, in an area of Canada which cannot stand this further blow to its economy.
This is a divisive regulation. It divides one Canadian against another. If federalism is to mean anything, if we in Atlantic Canada are to be considered part of the Dominion of Canada, then the Gulf of St. Lawrence is owned as much by Newfoundlanders and Nova Scotians as it is by anyone else. Either we are all Canadians and all share equally, or federalism as we know it no longer interests. However, this regulation would imply that Nova Scotians and Newfoundlanders do not have the same fishing rights in the Gulf of St. Lawrence as other Canadians. It seeks to imply that we are little more than second class citizens, a title which we do not, will not and cannot accept.
I say this regulation is indefensible because the government gave no notice of its plans to the Canadian fishing industry. It is indefensible because the government is robbing Canadians of a fishing right which it is not prepared to take away from foreign trawlers fishing in these same Canadian waters. For example, let us look at the agreement signed between Canada and France on March 27, 1972. Article 3 reads:
Fisheries
-fishing vessels registered in metropolitan France may continue to fish from January 15 to May 15 each year, up to May 15, 1986, on an equal footing with Canadian vessels in the Canadian fishing zone within the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
Foreign fleets are phased out, but Canadian fleets are ordered out by this cabinet and by this government. How in the name of reason can this be called a conservation measure when foreign fleets, fishing in the Gulf of St. Lawrence primarily for cod, will throw back into the sea hundreds of thousands of pounds of dead fish; flounder, redfish, yellowtail, or any other kind of fish caught in their trawls?
In my opinion this action is indefensible because the government has gone ahead with regulations without conducting an impact analysis of the effects of its actions on the economy of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. How many more fish plants must close down in Nova Scotia besides the four I already placed on record before the government wakes up and stops its nonsensical approach to this important primary industry?
The government's actions are indefensible because it announced control regulations before establishing a management plan for the fisheries on the Canadian continental shelf, a management plan which should project our fisheries objectives for no less than five and at least ten years ahead. We desperately need this plan for it was only in 1973 that government fisheries scientists were saying that redfish in the gulf were dying of old age.
The industry was told to modernize its trawlers and take advantage of these fish stocks. The industry did modernize. New ships and plants were built. New equipment was purchased. However, the government is now saying, "Sorry, gentlemen, you must cut back. You must shut down operations."

speechtext:
The minister says a minute or two.
The industry did modernize. It improved its operations. I say to this House that you cannot treat the fishing industry like a light switch. It does not turn on and off that easily. It is too big and its ancilliary industries are so massive that it is time the government recognized its importance by appointing a full time minister to look after its problems.
The Minister of State (Fisheries) has not provided this House or the industry with one shred of evidence to prove that the stocks of redfish have declined below the sustainable yield level. How many tests were made, and what scientists carried out the studies? How much intermingling is there of stocks of redfish inside and outside the gulf? How big are the schools of redfish that surge into the gulf from St. Pierre banks, when do those migrations occur, and how long do they last?
There are questions the minister will not or cannot answer because his regulations are based on conclusions reached by bureaucrats in the ivory towers of Ottawa. The government moved the mint to Winnipeg. In my opinion the fisheries department should have great presence in Atlantic Canada as well as on the west coast. Civil servants should get out of the city, go to where the action is, and work with the industry. They would quickly learn that the big need of this industry is not marketing, which seems to occupy so much time of the minister's staff, but rather the big requirement is resource management.
Instead of carrying out isolated resource management on one or two species, as is being done on haddock and redfish in the gulf, the government should, in fact must concentrate its efforts on managing all the stocks on our continental shelf. You simply cannot manage fish stocks by selecting one or two species in isolation from the rest.
Finally, 1976 must be the year of action on the management of fish stocks by Canada. We must give notice by June, 1976, of any change of intent to withdraw from ICNAF, six months' notice, before we can act to set up our own management for our 200 mile economic zone.
Unfortunately at this time the government has no management plan and no stock assessment. In fact, this government is in a panic on this issue. It is signing away phasing-out rights to other countries without actually knowing the quantity of the remaining resource. Treaties are being made with foreign countries on a ten year basis, but Canadians are not being given ten days' consultation.
The government's information from its scientists is limited, garbled, hazy and, in many cases, incorrect. Not one scientist accompanied the winter fleet into the gulf this year. Why not make a start today on a resource management analysis? Get the scientists out of Ottawa, contact the industry and place at least six men on six different boats in the deep sea fleet for six months. Let them make soundings, age tests of fish caught, size and quantity of fish caught in every two hour tow, and the species landed.
In conclusion, this industry deserves better treatment than being put out of business by the wrong decisions being made by the wrong people living in the wrong places.

speechtext:
Perhaps unsuccessful leadership candidates on the other side can draw a lesson from the success of their winning candidate who took a highly national view and thereby won national support at their leadership convention.
The fact is that the resources of the sea are not solely the concern of maritime members, but the concern of all Canadians, indeed of all the people of the world. The sooner we appreciate this the more importance these resources will be accorded in terms of public policy, and the greater recognition there will be by government that they must be managed with care.
As the Law of the Sea Conference resumes in New York next week I am sure all hon. members will wish to express support for our negotiating team, our representatives at that conference who have conducted themselves so well on behalf of Canada in the past and who will be doing so over the next few weeks as well. I believe we have a first class negotiating team, headed on the professional side by one of our outstanding public servants. It has had the leadership of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), and the former Secretary of State for External Affairs, the present President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp).
We have not been followers in this matter. We have been leaders, and I think we should be proud of the performance of our ministers and our public servants in the leadership
March 12, 1976

they have given to the world in the field of the rule of law in all matters pertaining to the sea.
I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs acknowledged, as I would like to do, that the mover of this motion, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) is motivated by a desire to support the negotiators at the conference. I am sure this is his desire. However, in dealing with the motion itself we must recognize that it is sadly deficient.
One needs only to listen to the spokesmen for the opposition to realize that the wording of the motion demonstrates as well as anything the difference between the approach of the government and of the opposition to Canada's foreign relations. The opposition seeks confrontation. The government seeks co-operation. It is surely apparent now, if it has never been in the past, that solutions to the interlocking world crises will not come about through expressions of self-interest on the part of each of us, but rather through a lot of hard work in co-operating among peoples and in improving respect for international law.
I admire the patience and the persistence which the government has shown in pursuing the establishment of the rule of law in matters pertaining to the sea and I believe all members, including the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, wish our negotiators success as they continue this very important work on behalf of Canada.
The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) emphasized the importance of having a strong voice speak for the fisheries of Canada. I believe we have that strong voice in the person of the Minister of State for Fisheries. We do need a full time Minister of Fisheries and we have a full time minister.
