subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext:
Well, if he is as effective and as hard working as he is at the pay he is getting I do not know that it would be fair to him to increase his pay, because he would feel he should work that much harder, and I don't think that is possible. He has been a most effective champion of Canadian fishermen, but beyond this he has been a most effective champion of the importance of the resources of the sea to all of us. This is something of which we must all become more conscious.
The motion before us says the government must unilaterally proclaim its exclusive jurisdication over a 200-mile coastal fisheries zone. This is the kind of gauntlet-throwing which does not contribute to progress in negotiations. It represents the ultimate option we may have to exercise, and the government has made it clear that we shall unilaterally proclaim a coastal fishing zone if necessary. But the motion says very little on close examination, and I suggest that to adopt it would achieve even less. To paraphrase the Minister of State for Fisheries who said in Geneva, "Fishermen cannot eat negotiating texts and fish stocks cannot be rebuilt with negotiating texts", I would suggest that fish stocks cannot be built on motions, nor can fishermen eat such motions.
Opposition spokesmen are ignoring what the government has already done and is doing for Canadian fishermen. This work is not about to start next week, Mr. Fisheries
Speaker. It began years ago. The Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned that in 1964 the government did take unilateral action to extend Canada's fishing limit to 12 miles. It did so as a last resort, only after all possibility of agreement had been exhausted. In 1970 the government went further and closed certain areas, reserving them as exclusive Canadian fishing zones, and negotiated phaseout agreements with countries affected. As a result very substantial foreign operations off our coasts are already coming to an end. I believe this demonstrates the kind of effective action the government is prepared to take without leading to a "cod war" or a challenge before the International Court of Justice. Those are very real dangers which the motion before us ignores.
Canada has taken a back seat to no nation in the law of the sea discussions. The reason we have succeeded as well as we have is that we have always gone that extra mile toward seeking international agreement before striking out on our own. We have done this not because we are Boy Scouts, though some of us may have been, but because we are realists. Canada is and continues to be in the vanguard of countries pressing for a further extension of fisheries jurisdiction. We have already gained overwhelming recognition for the concept of the 200-mile limit.
The Geneva session of the Law of the Sea Conference last spring did not result in a Law of the Sea Convention, but it did produce a single negotiating text which represents a very significant step forward in these proceedings. The fisheries articles of the text are deficient in some points in terms of our objectives, but they reflect our interests in most respects and offer a sound basis for further negotiations which are now under way in New York.
We hope that the Law of the Sea Conference can succeed this year, but in any event the Secretary of State for External Affairs has reiterated today the firm commitment of the government to a timely and effective extension of Canada's fisheries jurisdiction to 200 miles. While the government would prefer to extend jurisdiction on the basis of a new Law of the Sea Convention, it has not awaited the conclusion of that convention to take action.
The House will recall that last July the government closed Canada's Atlantic ports to the Soviet fishing fleet in response to evidence of overruns of quotas agreed in ICNAF. At the same time Spain and Portugal were warned that the same action would be taken against them if their adherence to the ICNAF regulations did not improve. The response was quite satisfactory; within two months arrangements had been negotiated with the USSR to establish procedures which should guarantee compliance with ICNAF arrangements in the future. Appropriate arrangements have also been worked out with Spain and Portugal.
For the 1976 fishing season the government recently obtained through ICNAF a 40 per cent reduction in foreign fishing efforts for groundfish as well as a reduction in the total allowable catches for depleted stocks and higher quotas for Canadian fishermen on stocks of particular importance to them. These measures are not a substitute for the 200-mile limit but they will help provide for a smooth transition to extended jurisdiction.

March 12, 1976
Fisheries
To prepare further the way for extension of jurisdiction, Canadian officials have begun discussions with a number of governments whose fishing operations will be affected by Canada's adoption of the 200-mile limit. These negotiations anticipate the results of the Law of the Sea Conference and are intended to fix the terms and conditions under which foreign vessels would be permitted to fish in Canada's extended fishing zones, under Canadian authority and control, for resources surplus to Canadian requirements as determined by Canada.
We are informed that bilateral agreements along these lines have already been negotiated with Norway, Poland, Spain, and only yesterday with Portugal. In other words we have in place agreements that cover some 30 per cent of the total foreign catch in the ICNAF area off the Canadian coast, and an agreement with the USSR would bring this figure up to 88 per cent.
Surely it is important, Mr. Speaker, that Canada's extension of jurisdiction be achieved in such a way as to avoid "cod war" confrontations and keep enforcement costs to a manageable level. We do not want the kind of confrontation with other countries that has been cited with approval by members opposite.
I believe the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) interjected, while the minister was speaking, that Iceland has demonstrated she can take on Britain. Does the opposition really want Canada to have to demonstrate that she can take on Britain, or any other country? Surely not! This is a time when the rule of law should be improved in the world and extended, not a time for the rule of force.
At least for the present, negotiations offer many advantages and no disadvantages. The timing of the actual extension of jurisdiction will be important, but the government is now doing everything that could be done after extension of jurisdiction to make this extension truly effective. Whatever may happen in coming months the steps now being taken will contribute to the early attainment of Canadian objectives.
A so-called unilateral declaration is an option which could be exercised at very short notice in view of the fact that the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act empowers the government to extend further Canada's fisheries jurisdiction by simple order in council. Thus, unlike such countries as the U.S.A., Mexico and Norway, Canada has long had in place the necessary enabling legislation for adoption of the 200-mile limit.
We must continue our efforts to reach international agreement on fisheries problems at the Law of the Sea Conference, through ICNAF and other international fisheries commissions as well as through bilateral negotiations. I suggest that these efforts are not incompatible with other forms of action that may prove necessary. Indeed they would prepare the way for such forms of action. There is a limit not only to our patience but to the ability of stocks and our fishing industry to survive under present conditions.
Unilateral action is one of the options open to us. However, even unilateral action requires negotiation if it is to be effective and successful, as it was when Canada moved unilaterally in 1964 and 1970. It is always tempting to take

unilateral action, but unilateral action is not particularly rewarding unless it can be made to work. No government in this country or in any other country has demonstrated greater concern for the fisheries and fishermen and the resources of the sea than has the present Government of Canada. No government has done more than ours in the way of both national and international action to protect coastal fisheries and coastal fishermen.
We know that the future of our coastal communities is inseparably linked with the future of our fisheries, and I might go so far as to say with the future of all Canadian communities, and indeed of mankind. We intend not only to protect that future but to make it better than ever. We will take the measures that are necessary, but we will always act, I hope, in a responsible, reasonable, and realistic manner. We owe it to ourselves and to our fishermen to proceed in this way.
We are almost home, Mr. Speaker, and it would be folly at this point, simply for the sake of a dramatic entrance, to break down the door that is already opening.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member who just spoke before me stated, we have almost made it home. History tells me we have known for many years that Jack did make it down the beanstalk with the golden goose, but I am not quite so sure our minister is as nimble, and I think, having heard him today, he may be caught in his own bear trap which he set at the bottom of the stalk.
Canada has set forward two thrusts in international negotiations in the past few years. We have been engaged in bilateral negotiations and in a unilateral declaration of the 200-mile limit. Although I do not predict this I wonder whether history will show that in our enthusiasm we have been too hasty and aggressive on the one count, and too slow on the other. It is not too many years ago that in British Columbia we climbed out of the hills after having gotten on a ladder, and having arrived at the top we found we had given away 50 per cent of the salmon run on a great river.
As the Canadian negotiators climbed that ladder I imagine they felt quite enthusiastic, smug, and self-satisfied that Canada was getting a good deal. I am sure they must have felt that way in respect of the negotiations on the Columbia River Treaty and the Skagit River Treaty. I am concerned, however, about that attitude.
The minister tells us we have in some way almost won the battle; that we have signed spectacular agreements with Norway, Portugal, Poland, and Spain and that he is pretty sure Russia will get to her knees and give us a tremendous deal. Personally I have some question about that. I would be suspicious under any circumstances, but having heard the minister today I am even more suspicious. While I agree in principle with the philosophy of dealing with cod wars and this type of thing through negotiated settlements, I wonder whether by taking that course of action we might well be sealing our heritage in vested sovereign rights unnecessarily and prematurely.
Any negotiation indicates a give and take. I ask the minister what we are giving up? What are they taking for these agreements? As I looked at the agreement with
March 12, 1976

Norway I thought it looked a progressive step because it stated very simply that Norwegian vessels would be permitted to fish in the area concerned under Canadian authority and control for resources surplus to Canadian requirements. That is pretty easy to agree to but today we have started to find out what really is behind the agreement. We have started to find out not only that we are talking about a surplus of Canadian fisheries requirements but are dividing that surplus up in given percentages. We have already given away percentages.
The minister made some sort of statement - at least I thought he did and I would ask him if he made the statement - that Norway, Poland, Portugal, and Spain have agreements, and that at the time we finish with Russia we will have given away the right to 88 per cent of our surplus. He shakes his head. I will be interested in hearing his explanation of that. At any rate he is giving away a guaranteed percentage of our fishing surplus.
That statement requires clarification because if we give away 88 per cent that leaves 12 per cent. Is that 12 per cent for East Germany, for the Koreas, and for the Third World? Is this not a dangerous and greedy precedent? That is certainly an area which the minister will have to clarify, and I will try to finish my speech as quickly as I can so that he will have that opportunity. I suggest that well might be the bear trap. If you give away 88 per cent here and 12 per cent there, you still have not mentioned the requirement of the Third World countries, the Koreas, East Germany or other areas.
I suggest that perhaps in his negotiations the minister should include some kind of a Third World option so that if these percentages are to be determined there will be a way out of them. Again, so far as I can see, he was talking about a surplus. I want to know, if he is referring to a surplus beyond Canadian requirements, where the requirements, of the United States come into the picture. Does he include the requirements of the United States and Canada as one and the same? Then I question, if he is already talking about giving away a majority or the greater part of our surplus, who it is being given to and how it is being given to them.
The rationale seems to be to ensure that our 200-mile limit will be respected. I am not sure I like to have it respected in that order of precedence. I think I might have preferred to see the precedence first through bilateral negotiations with the United States, our traditional friend and supporter. At any rate I am sure the minister will have some clarification in this regard. If he is walking into this trap, I urge caution. I urge him not to be too hasty in further negotiations with Russia. I urge him to be cautious in this area.
The time to be aggressive is in the declaration of the 200-mile limit. That is where he is moving cautiously. I ask him to move in that direction. This in effect is what this motion talks about. I do not in any way underrate not only the important implication of this 200-mile limit but also the effect it will have on the Canadian body of law and Canadian fishermen. Of course I support it. I do not underestimate its significance as a step forward in enlarging, and focusing on, the direction of international law. The implications for international law here surely are as great as the implications for fishing or for Canada itself.
Fisheries
But as I see Canada and our minister participating in this great international arena, and as I see him floundering when he says we have much planning to do in Canada before we are ready to make a declaration, I say that if we wait for the planning in Canada we will wait forever because there is so much that needs to be done at home. We might look at one absurd example. We talk in terms of international agreement and of us being a dominant factor in showing leadership and innovation. Yet this is a country which cannot even decide who has jurisdiction for the safety of our fishermen. I point out this is an absurdity, and question the ability of the minister in the broader and much more difficult problems which cannot be solved this simply.
In essence the problem stems from the fact that the federal and provincial governments have neglected to institute safety programs for the fishing fleets to prevent further loss of life on the coast of British Columbia. The situation is drastic and the outcome inevitable if the federal government insists on delaying safety provisions any longer. Last year some 14 lives were lost during the herring season alone, and some 13 vessels either capsized or went down. I think those 14 lives have some value and warrant the minister's time, concern, and energy. Those are the important values. So far this season one life has been lost and six vessels have either capsized or gone down. This was in the herring season alone and we can cite statistics in other areas.
This concern is recognized, but Ottawa is so busy playing little games that the provincial government tries to step in by bringing in Workmen's Compensation Board regulations overlapping and intruding on federal jurisdiction, with hundreds of pages of regulations which cannot possibly be met and might do more harm to individual fishermen than protect them as workers. Certainly that problem needs to be straightened out. Federal inspection has long been the responsibility of MOT and is clearly and historically a matter of federal jurisdiction. Any change in the regulations should be made through these channels. A separate and unrelated government department also inspecting fishing vessels is certainly not required.
There is no need for this loss of life and property which I have mentioned, and which goes on while we negotiate elsewhere. Fishermen, and more specifically the fishermen's union on the west coast, have urged the federal government for some years now to give this matter its immediate attention. The fishermen's proposals are most acceptable and quite logical. They are simply asking for a more effective air-sea rescue squad. This squad, which already exists, could be supplemented by the use of all available vessels, helicopters, and fixed-wing aircraft in the immediate vicinity. These other vessels exist in the form of RCMP boats, naval vessels, and naval helicopters. Certainly it would seem that in times of tragedy or possible death using these available vessels in an organized, effective, and efficient way is the only recourse and logical step of action.
Canadian fishermen are too often forced to rely on their U.S. counterparts for air-sea rescue. Their forces are well equipped, they are efficient, and Canada could learn much from them. Perhaps on his next international foray the

March 12, 1976
Fisheries
minister could take some time to find out about the simple problem of the safety of our fishermen and inquire of his U.S. counterparts how they can be so much more efficient and competent in this area.
It is no secret that these fishermen-

speechtext:
I suggested a trip to the United States where he can meet with the delegates and obtain some information for our fishermen.
It is no secret that these fishermen who have a great deal of overhead are not well off by today's standards. These same fishermen on the west coast have asked for federal assistance grants to supplement their income. These grants are not for frills or lavish accessories for their vessels. These grants would be used for better equipping and reinforcing their boats and communications equipment. Constant communication is an absolute necessity in times of disaster. It is their only link to life.
These same fishermen, represented by their union, were quite prepared to sit down with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc), and whatever power the cabinet can muster to look at this problem. Their intention was to meet with these ministers jointly with the minister of labour from British Columbia and representatives from the ministry of transport in British Columbia. Their plans were scuttled in every instance. I think those ministers responsible should plan to solve this problem expeditiously. It is not understating the situation to say that the lives of 7,000 people in British Columbia fishermen's union are at stake.
While I encourage aggressiveness in the declaration of the 200 mile, I also encourage caution in bilateral negotiations where a government may well be giving away our heritage. I ask the minister to qualify that. I wish the minister success in these negotiations, and although many say that the minister's efforts will not be fully rewarded and fruitful I am sure that Canada's position will be well expressed by a competent negotiating team. I hope the minister will listen to them and act accordingly.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Iona Campagnolo (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FISHERIES-SUGGESTED PROCLAMATION OF 200-MILE COASTAL ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that the speech which I had prepared for today cannot be delivered but I hope in the three minutes I have, to express the concerns of the people on the northwest coast in British Columbia as they relate to the opposition motion of today, which requests that an extension of Canada's territorial waters by 200 miles be undertaken unilaterally by Canada. This brings to mind many reasonable concerns of fishermen and mariners on the north coast of British Columbia because, of course, one of the major enterprises of that part of the world is the anadromous species on which we have heard a great deal of discussion at the Law of the Sea conferences.
When we have salmon which come to life in the waters of our rivers, which go to sea and know no restraints in their travels across the seas-there are also herring and other types of anadromous species-they do not stop at the 200-mile limit, turn around and come back in, but go much farther out to sea than the 200 miles. Therefore it is

essential that in the negotiations that are taking place in New York, and that have taken place in Caracas and Geneva, the anadromous species be absolutely and completely cared for so that management of high seas fisheries by Canada can continue beyond the 200-mile limit.
What we are waiting for until we have negotiated a reasonable status for the high seas salmon and other anadromous species is that we make certain, beyond the 200 mile limit, that they are still under our economic control and that we have an economic zone of influence over these fish. I feel that it would be absolutely foolhardy to make a unilateral attendant upon our seas. What are we going to do about surveillance? Will we have one, single, unified coastguard in this country? Unless we do, I submit it will be impossible for us to declare unilaterally a 200-mile limit.
I cannot understand why the opposition finds it necessary to come up with this disease every once in a while of precipitous unilateralism, the symptoms of which are absolute myopia.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-MINISTERIAL CONDUCT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) tabled a report of the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Quebec with regard to allegations that certain ministers of the government had approached judges of the Superior Court of Quebec during the course of the last few years.
In the case five years ago of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) the Chief Justice concurred with the view of the judge concerned that while the approach in question was not proper practice, it did not constitute interference or intervention calling for formal protest and he recommends that the incident should be considered closed.
In the case involving the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) before he was elected to this House and while he was employed in the Prime Minister's Office six years ago, Mr. Justice Mackay decided not to take any formal action because it was clearly inspired by great concern for the nation's interest and not by personal reasons. The Chief Justice describes the approach as unusual-insolite is the word in French-but also believes this file should not be reopened.
In the recent case of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury), while the associate chief justice did not regard the approach as an attempt to influence his judgment and so took no action, he did regard the approach, despite its good
March 12, 1976

intentions, as improper, and the Chief Justice found the facts related grave, given the stature of the person making the call and the circumstances in which the call was made. In the light of this finding the minister last night tendered to me his resignation.
After receiving the report of the Chief Justice, I consulted the Minister of Justice to ascertain if it contained any information which would justify the laying of formal charges of interference in the judicial process. I have been advised by the minister that it is the opinion of the law officers of the Crown that in none of the cases do they find grounds for charges that any of the ministers concerned acted illegally.
To conclude that there has not been illegal action is not, however, to say that there has been no impropriety. Indeed, in the case of the Minister of Public Works the Chief Justice has noted the gravity of the facts which led Mr. Justice Hugessen to regard the call to him as improper, however well motivated it may have been.
Had the associate chief justice felt the matter so serious as to take formal action to have it reported at the time to the Chief Justice, and through him to me or to the Minister of Justice, there is no doubt that I would have taken immediate steps to have an investigation made and, in the light of what was revealed, would if necessary have requested the resignation of the minister. I entirely concur with the view of the Chief Justice that the independence of the judiciary must remain protected from interventions from members of the cabinet, whatever may be the quality of the intentions which inspire them, and I believe the course of action I have described is the appropriate one which should be followed where members of the judiciary perceive that their independence is in any way being affected by members of the executive.
But the associate chief justice clearly was of the view that the call from the Minister of Public Works did not warrant formal protest. I do not excuse the minister's lapse of judgment in this matter. I sympathize with his good intentions, but I do not condone what he did. We have heard his apology this morning, and the way in which hon. members in all parties in this House received his apology and spoke of his distinguished career. After considering his long service to this House and to our country, and his well recognized stature as a man of honour without peer amongst us, I have come to the conclusion that I should not accept his resignation.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-MINISTERIAL CONDUCT
speechtext: Nothing further would be gained by my acceptance of it, and much would most assuredly be lost, not only to the government but to parliament and to Canada.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
As regards the other two cases, though the judges concerned did not feel that any formal action should be taken and the Chief Justice has concluded that these incidents should be considered closed, I believe them to be sufficiently serious to warrant not only the sincere regret which the President of the Treasury Board and the
Ministerial Conduct
Minister of National Health and Welfare, expressed this morning, but also that there should be an immediate clarification of the regime which under this and, I hope, any future government will govern the relationship of members of the cabinet with members of the judiciary.
I agree with the Chief Justice that the independence of the judiciary is a cornerstone of our democratic system and must be jealously guarded against all attacks. Indeed, I would go further and say that we must do what we can to avoid affecting the principle of judicial independence with even the appearance of possible compromise.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-MINISTERIAL CONDUCT
speechtext: Gee!

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-MINISTERIAL CONDUCT
speechtext:
This clearly must not be achieved by saying that ministers may have no contact with judges. That would be ridiculous, not only for its effects on purely social relationships but also because a number of ministers must in the course of their duties discuss matters of government business with members of the judiciary. Indeed, it is clear that the rules on contact with judges vary somewhat not only in what they say, but in how they are customarily applied in the various jurisdictions of this country. Some hon. members of this House may even have different views as to what their duties to their constituents require them to do from time to time in getting in touch with judges.
But, in so far as this government is concerned, I believe that it must be clearly established that in future no member of the cabinet may communicate with members of the judiciary concerning any matter which they have before them in their judicial capacities, except through the Minister of Justice, his duly authorized officials or counsel acting for him, nor may any member of the cabinet communicate with members of quasi-judicial bodies which are constituted as courts of record concerning any matter which they have before them in their judicial capacities except through the minister responsible, his duly authorized officials, or counsel acting for him.
I turn now to the matter of public inquiry, such as is being requested by the opposition. I continue to hold the view that such inquiries are, by definition, related to inquisitory concepts of justice and should not be resorted to except when the rule of law cannot be relied upon to ensure that justice is done.
In the present case, in so far as relations between certain ministers and judges are concerned, the facts are known since both the ministers and judges have from personal knowledge stated those facts, it is also known that in the opinion of the law officers of the Crown those facts do not give rise to criminal or contempt action.
In so far as relations between ministers themselves are concerned, I stated this morning and I repeat now that, in my view, the privacy of conversations between any two individuals in society should be respected, except when the greater good of society demands otherwise. Since it is not improper to seek counsel and advice from a friend, even be he a minister, in any grave matter of personal concern, and since there is no reason to believe, nor has anyone in this House or outside alleged, that any conversation between ministers has resulted in any crime or conspiracy, there is no prima facie case to demand that secrecy of private communications be broken.

March 12, 1976
Ministerial Conduct
For these reasons, unless allegations or facts are brought to my attention of which I presently know nothing, I conclude that there is no need in this case for a public inquiry.

Thus the clear possibility remains that one minister of the Crown directly requested another minister of the Crown to interfere in the judicial process. Without a public inquiry that whole relationship, that whole course of events, will remain obscure. The people of Canada, the people out there, outside the House, who want some ground for respecting our parliamentary government and who support the separation of the judiciary from the executive, will remain cynical. They will say, "This is a cover-up; there they are, those powerful people. They make the law; they implement the law. They even mingle with the judiciary; and they get away with violations." Cab drivers, fishermen, and other working people know in their hearts that they would not get away with such violations.

The Honourable Jules Deschenes,

Dear Chief Justice Deschenes:
You will be aware that in his letter to me dated February 20, 1976, Mr. Justice Mackay drew to my attention three incidents which, in his view, constituted unwarranted attempts by Ministers of the Government of Canada to interfere with the judicial process in cases that were before judges of the Superior Court of the Province of Quebec.
As I indicated in my remarks in the House of Commons yesterday which are set out in the enclosed copy of the Debates, I feel that this is a matter on which I, as Minister of Justice should communicate with you as Chief Justice of the Court in question. In this regard, you will note that the transcript of the debates makes reference throughout
to the Chief Justice of the Province of Quebec; it should of course refer to the Chief Justice of the Superior Court.
My reason for believing that the communication should be with you is set forth in the Debates. Put simply, I feel that if there is information indicating that anyone is or has been seeking improperly to interfere with the due admini-tration of justice in a court, by approaches to a judge or otherwise, this is a matter of which the Chief Justice of the Court, as the judge principally responsible for the management of the Court and for protecting its independence and integrity, would be made fully aware.
I am therefore writing to you to invite you to draw to my attention, if you deem such action appropriate, information that may be in your possession respecting any unwarranted attempts to interfere with the proper administration of justice in your Court in respect of matters that should be of concern to me.
Yours sincerely,
Ron Basford.

subsubtopic: CHIEF JUSTICE SUPERIOR COURT OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
By your letter of March 4 last, you forwarded to me an invitation which, in its essential parts, read as follows:
"My reason for believing that the communication should be with you is set forth in the Debates. Put simply, I feel that if there is information indicating tht anyone is or has been seeking improperly to interfere with the due administration of justice in a court, by approaches to a judge or otherwise, this is a matter of which thee Chief Justice of the Court, as the judge principally responsible for the management of the Court and for protecting its independence and integrity, would be made fully aware.
I am therefore writing to you to invite you to draw to my attention, if you deem such action appropriate, information that may be in your possession respecting any unwarranted attempts to interfere with the proper administration of justice in your Court in respect of matters that should be of concern to me."
This invitation was extended against the background of allegations which had recently been made public to the effect that on three occasions Ministers of the Government of Canada had approached judges of the Superior Court of Quebec during the course of the last few years.
At the outset it is important to recall the basic principles which govern the relations between the judiciary and the other two branches of government in our country.
The British North America Act of 1867 deals with the executive branch in chapter III, the legislative branch in chapter IV and the judiciary (Judicature) in chapter VIII.
Sections 96, 99 and 100 of the B.N.A. Act assure the judiciary the guarantees of independence and security which are essential to its impartiality and which have been guaranteed by long tradition
since the Act of Settlement of 1700 (12-13 William III, Chapter 2),
notwithstanding the Constitutional Act of 1791 (31 George III, Chapter 31),
in conformity with the recommendation of Lord Durham in his Report of January 31, 1839 (Lucas, II, page 327)
and by virtue of the two acts enacted under the Union in 1843 (7 Victoria, Chapter 15 and Chapter 65).
It is of the utmost importance that this independence of the judiciary, achieved through great effort during the course of the last three centuries, be jealously guarded against all attacks.
March 12, 1976
More particularly, it must remain protected from interventions from Members of the Cabinet, whatever may be the quality of the intentions that inspire them.
It remains to add, in the light of recent events that it must also be protected from interventions from Parliament. I can do no better than to recall the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the House of Commons on September 15, 1903:
"It is a strange doctrine to preach that the judges are responsible to Parliament. Where is that responsibility? I have always understood that the judges were responsible only to their own conscience, and Parliament has no power over them. True, they can be removed, but only on an address of both Houses of Parliament. That law has been adopted to make them absolutely independent of Parliament, and they are only responsible to Parliament in extreme cases of malfeasance."
(Can. H. of C. Debates, Sept. 15, 1903, p. 11313).
Within this system, certain persons hold the responsibility for ensuring the integrity and the efficacy of the functioning of the judicial system.
From the outset, considering the nature of the events which cause me to write to you and in order to avoid any confusion, it seems to me that we must discard any suggestion that the Canadian Judicial Council has a role to play in this matter, its jurisdiction relates to an examination of complaints relating to the conduct of judges and not to complaints that might concern the conduct of third parties in relation to them. (Judges Act, 1970 R.S.C. chapter J-l, section 30-32).
This having been said, the Department of Justice Act (1970 R.S.C. chapter J-2) provides in section 4 that "The Minister of Justice shall
c) have the superintendence of all matters connected with the administration of justice in Canada, not within the jurisdiction of the governments of the provinces;"
On the other hand, my duties as Chief Justice are described in part in section 21a of the Courts of Justice Act of Quebec (1964 R.S.Q., chapter 20, as amended by 1974 S.Q. chapter 11, section 13):
"21a. The Chief Justice, the Senior Associate Chief Justice and the Associate Chief Justice of the Superior Court shall coordinate and apportion the work of the judges of such court.
The judges of such court shall be under the supervision of the Chief Justice, the Senior Associate Chief Justice and of the Associate Chief Justice and must comply with their orders and directives as regards the carrying out of their work.
March 12, 1976

Such paragraphs apply subject to the provisions which follow."
As everyone knows however, this statutory provision describes but one part of the total duties of the Chief Justice, and that his duties derive even more from unwritten practice and tradition.
One thing is certain, I have a profound concern for the integrity of the Superior Court, the independence of its members and the efficacy of its work.
There exists then a definite point of contact between your obligations and mine, though they may come from different sources: it is for this reason that I consider it my duty to respond to your invitation.
I consider myself however under no obligation in relation to Parliament-save that of good behaviour-nor towards the government and the invitations to undertake an inquiry which have been addressed to me in the House of Commons appear to me to be out of place.
Even more out of place appears to me to be the suggestion, also expressed in the House of Commons, that there would exist a "cosy 'All in the family' arrangement" (H. of C. Deb., March 4, 1976, page 11490).
I can also only dismiss the proposition that I proceed to interview privately one or other Members of the Cabinet whose names were mentioned in the House. I was not appointed to conduct a commission of inquiry and of course it is obviously not one of my functions to set myself up as a semi-official investigator on behalf of the House of Commons.
I have therefore not met with your colleagues nor had the least contact with them, either directly or indirectly.
I have learned through the media, these past few days, the allegations of unwarranted interventions that the Honourable Judge Kenneth C. Mackay forwarded to you by letter of February 20, 1976 concerning the Honourable Marc Lalonde, the Honourable Jean Chretien and the Honourable Charles M. Drury.
These are obviously matters of concern to me, and concerned me as soon as they came to my attention. I must point out however that no one had made the least mention of them to me before the reports of the Globe & Mail of Toronto on March 3. Moreover, the first two incidents arose during the term of my predecessor who, to the best of my knowledge, had not been made aware of them, at least officially.
I therefore do not want to set myself up here as a judge neither of your colleague nor of mine. But in view of the publicity that these incidents have attracted and considering the effect that they are likely to have on the conception that the public holds and should hold concerning the administration of justice, I believe it opportune to forward to you the information that I have so that you may, in respect of your responsibilities, adopt such measures as appear to you to be appropriate. I will do the same, as may be appropriate, within the sphere of my responsibilities.
The three incidents arose in the Province of Quebec and involved three members of the Bar. It therefore appears to be in order to recall certain rules which regulate the conduct of lawyers.
Section 2 of the Bar Act (1967 S.Q. chapter 77) came into force on June 29, 1967 and has not since been amended:
"2. An advocate is an officer of the court and participates in the administration of justice.
2. L'avocat exerce une fonction publique aupres du tribunal et collabore a l'administration de la justice."
Regulation number 1 of the Bar of Quebec was adopted on October 20, 1967 and came into force on February 1, 1968. The sections which follow, taken from this regulation, have not been amended since:
"29. 1. An advocate must serve justice and uphold the authority of the Courts. He must never compromise the honour and dignity of the Bar. He must be faithful to his clients and honest and courteous to other advocates. So he must scrupulously discharge the duties imposed by the rules, traditions and customs of the profession."
"43. 3. In the absence or without the knowledge of the other party or of his advocate, he shall not make, before judgment or decision, on behalf of a party in a contested matter, any verbal or written representations to a judge, a court or the members of a judicial or quasi-judicial body."
"68. An advocate shall not, by fraudulent or illegal acts, try to prevent that justice be done."
I now propose to deal briefly with each one of the incidents in question.
One of them involved the Honourable Jean Chretien and Mr. Justice Harry L. Aronovitch, in the fall of 1971.
Mr. Justice Aronovitch has provided me with the following description of the event which he has authorized me to transmit to you:
"On September 30, 1971, I heard the following matters: 1. Petition to ratify proposal; 2. Opposition to ratification of proposal; 3. Motion to delay ratification of proposal. At the termination of the hearing, it was agreed that written notes were to be submitted within one week, and, then, I was to make all the afore said matters under advisement.
Some time in October 1971, Mr. Jean Chretien, whom I did not (and still do not) know, telephoned to find out when I would render judgment. He identified himself to me, not as a cabinet minister, but as a member of Parliament interested in the people in his riding or constituency where apparently the petitioner was operating.
As occurs on the rare occasion when such a call is received from a lawyer, I told him that I would render judgment when ready, or something to that effect. In any event, as I recall, I made it clear that his telephoning me would have no bearing on the date of the judgment which, again, was the only subject raised in the call.

March 12, 1976
I subsequently conveyed my feelings to some of our colleagues, at lunch, but did not consider the matter serious enough to report it to the Chief Justice; that is, while I consider the telephone call was not proper practice, I did not consider it to be interference or intervention calling for formal protest.
On November 3, 1971, my judgment was drafted, and on November 9, 1971, judgments were signed whereby I ratified the propoasl, as amended, dismissed the opposition, as well as the Motion to delay the ratification."
I share the views of Mr. Justice Aronovitch and, like him, I consider that the incident should be considered closed.
The second incident involved Mr. Marc Lalonde, at that time employed in the Prime Minister's office, and Mr. Justice MacKay.
Mr. Justice MacKay provided me with the version of the facts which he has authorized me to transmit to you:
"On Friday, March 6, 1970, the Crown led by Mr. Fred Kaufman (as he then was), completed its address to the jury sitting in the trial of Regina v. Robinson and eleven other persons accused of several charges of conspiracy arising out of the destruction of a computer at Sir George Williams University in 1969. I dined out that evening and when I arrived at my home at 3275 Cedar Avenue, I found that there was a message to call Mr. Marc Lalonde with whom I was slightly acquainted. The message gave no particulars as to the reasons for the call and I decided to call him in the morning. When I called there was no answer. During the day I worked in the library of my home on the preparation of my address to the jury. When I completed my work for that day-it was about six I would say-I called Mr. Lalonde again. He said he had been skiing with his family that day but would like to .. . drop around and see me the next day, which was Sunday. No reason was given for his wish to see me and both my wife and I were curious as to the purpose of such a visit. I did know of course that he was in charge of the Prime Minister's office, and we conjectured that it might have something to do with the possibility of another appointment.
In any event, late on Sunday morning, while I was working in my library, Mr. Lalonde arrived and I greeted him cordially, gave him a drink and mentioned that he was fortunate to have been able to ski the day before although he must find it awkward to rush down every weekend to be with his family since his many duties must interfere with this. We then exchanged a few more such banalities in French, which was the language in which our entire conversation was conducted.
He then came to the point of his visit: he told me that on Friday a telegram had been sent to the Prime Minister by Prime Minister Williams of Trinidad in which the latter had said that if the accused-who were natives of Trinidad-were found guilty before he
could get control of the local disturbed situation, that there was a very real possibility of a violent uprising in Trinidad. Mr. Lalonde said that when the telegram was received the Prime Minister had already taken off for a skiing holiday in the West, but that he- Lalonde-and others in the Prime Minister's office felt that the situation was so serious that it was decided to see me with a view to delaying the jury's decision. He pointed out that Canada had many interests in Trinidad and that these might well be affected if an uprising occurred in that country. I told him that I was about to charge the jury the next day and that there was nothing I could or would do to delay the jury's decision. I also told him that due to the complexity of the charges it would in my opinion be unlikely that a jury would come to any decision until the end of the week at the earliest. He repeated that the situation was one of grave concern.
As I showed him out we exchanged a few more general comments. The interview lasted for at least thirty minutes and although it continued to be cordial I was, inwardly at least, disturbed by this visit. Not only did I feel that I was being asked to see that the jury's decision was delayed, but that if for any reason the defence attorneys learned of the visit there was a possibility of a mistrial after an arduous and expensive eight week trial. I expressed this concern to my wife and requested that nothing be said about the visit at least until after the case was concluded.
I would add that I also decided not to say anything further about the matter, because Mr. Lalonde's visit was clearly inspired by his great concern for the nation's interests and not by personal reasons.
I subsequently reported this incident to a few of my colleagues including the late Associate Chief Justice Challies. But I did no informally after the case had been disposed of. I also told two or three friends who are members of the Bar.
I enclose my entire file relating to this matter. If some references may cause you offence I regret it, but as I have already assured you, all these letters were sent with the certainty that they would be read only by the recipients. I might also say that my purpose in bringing up the incidents set out in my letter to Mr. Basford, was simply to reply with particulars to the question he put in his letter to me. Although I was shocked to learn that my correspondence had been leaked to the press, nevertheless I believe that the publicity will have at least one beneficial effect. Never again will a member of the executive branch of the Government communicate with a judge about a case which he is trying."
I do not know the Honourable Marc Lalonde's version of the facts and I therefore do not wish to pass judgment on his conduct.
However, considering the particular circumstances surrounding this affair, I understand Mr. Justice Mackay's reaction in face of this unusual approach and I do not believe that it behooves me, six years later, to reopen the file.
March 12, 1976

The last incident involved, approximately two months ago, the Honourable Charles M. Drury and the Associate Chief Justice James K. Hugessen.
I can do no better than to transmit to you, with his authorization, Mr. Justice Hugessen's recital of the events that he provided to me on March 5:
"Mr. Drury telephoned me during the hearing of the contempt proceedings against Andre Ouellet. The call came to my home, in the evening, after dinner, when I was in the basement helping my youngest son to assemble a model train set which he had received for his birthday, a few days before. I took the call where I was and did not make any notes of it. The date was between the first and second days of the hearing, which were respectively January 8 and January 16, 1976. I am almost certain that the actual date of the call was Wednesday, January 14.
I have known Mr. Drury for many years and, while we are not intimate, we are on first-name terms.
The conversation dealt with two aspects of the Ouellet case:
1.	Whether it would be possible for Mr. Ouellet to make a formal apology and thereby bring the proceedings to an end, and
2.	The view which Mr. Drury felt was being expressed in some quarters in Ottawa that the proceedings against Mr. Ouellet were in some way a ganging up of the English speaking Establishment against prominently placed French speaking persons.
With regard to the first point, I simply told Mr. Drury that a person accused of contempt could always attempt to purge his offence by making a full and complete apology and that any such action would undoubtedly be taken into account by the Court in its final disposition of the matter. I also told him that the working out of the terms of the apology and any related matters should be discussed between counsel in the case and that I should not be involved until counsel had reached an agreement and were prepared to see me jointly. In fact, I had had ... a rather similar discussion with both counsel in my chambers immediately before the case started, on January 8. In both cases, the discussion was very short and came to an end when, in the first case, Mr. Ouellet's counsel and, in the second case, Mr. Drury said that Mr. Ouellet denied having spoken the words attributed to him. Since an apology would necessarily involve an admission of the words alleged, any further discussion was futile.
On the second point raised by Mr. Drury, I simply told him that I had never heard of any such thing, that I considered it to be ridiculous, and that, in any event, as a judge these matters were completely beyond my competence and I could not even consider them.
While I felt at the time that the call was improper (and I believe I said so to Mr. Drury), I did not think that he was attempting to influence my judgment. I rather had the impression that he was attempting, if possible, to head off a confrontation between the executive and judicial branches of government. In any event, rightly or wrongly, I did not take any action with regard to the call and dismissed it from my mind. To the extent that one can determine one's own mental processes, I am quite convinced that the call did not influence my decision one way or the other."
In fact, as you know, Mr. Justice Hugessen upheld the request for a citation for contempt of court by judgment dated January 23, 1976, which judgment is now under appeal.
I have little doubt that the facts related by Mr. Justice Hugessen are grave, considering the stature of the person making the call and the circumstances in which the call was made to him.
However, I do not know the Honourable Mr. Drury's version of the facts and I imagine there were no witnesses to the event.
Therefore, I abstain from passing judgment, except to note that Mr. Justice Hugessen played but a passive role here and was the victim of circumstances.
These are, Mr. Minister, the facts that I consider it my duty to bring to your attention.
Considering the very special circumstances that have surrounded the revelation of these incidents and the debates in Parliament to which they have given rise, I have no objections to your making this letter public, if you consider that appropriate. My three colleagues whose version of the events is set out above, have also consented to the publication of this letter.
Indeed I would see some advantage in doing so, so that the public may be reassured of the integrity of the judiciary, in view of the negative results of the approaches of which my colleagues were the object.
Yours truly,
Chief Justice, (signed) Jules Deschenes
Quebec, March 10, 1976.
Chief Justice Deschenes submitted this account to me in my capacity of Senior Associate Chief Justice of the Superior Court especially responsible for the administration of the Superior Court in the Quebec Appeal Division.
After consideration and discussion, I agree entirely with the views expressed by my colleague.
Senior Associate Chief Justice, (signed) Eugene Marquis

Monday March 15, 1976
